name: Sapta Purī (the seven liberating cities)
summary: The seven cities — Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Māyā (Haridvāra), Kāśī, Kāñcī, Avantikā (Ujjayinī) and Dvārakā — named in a widely recited Sanskrit verse as the places that grant liberation (mokṣa); a pan-Indian pilgrimage set rather than a single route.
details:
The list is usually quoted from a verse that runs “ayodhyā mathurā māyā kāśī kāñcī avantikā / purī dvāravatī caiva saptaitā mokṣadāyikāḥ” (recited in later Purāṇic and stotra literature; the earliest textual locus is not verified here). Two of the seven (Kāñcī and Kāśī) are also the seats of major Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava temple clusters; Haridvāra and Ujjayinī are two of the four Kumbha Melā sites.

The network is recorded here as MEMBER_OF edges from place records. The cities themselves are ancient, but the grouping is a devotional and geographical construct; scholars of sacred geography treat it as one of several overlapping pan-Indian schemes (Char Dhām, the twelve jyotirliṅgas, the Śakti pīṭhas).
limits: The verse that defines the seven is widely recited but its earliest textual source is not verified here; membership in the set says nothing about the age of any particular monument in the cities.
openQuestions: Earliest dated text that gives the seven-city verse.

name: Pañca Kedāra (five Kedāras of Garhwal)
summary: Five Śiva shrines in the Garhwal Himalaya — Kedārnāth, Tuṅgnāth, Rudranāth, Madhyamaheśvar and Kalpeśvar — joined by a legend in which Śiva, fleeing the Pāṇḍavas in the form of a bull, reappears in five parts at the five sites.
details: In the regional legend the Pāṇḍavas seek Śiva to expiate the killing of kin at Kurukṣetra; Śiva hides as a bull and sinks into the ground at Kedārnāth, leaving the hump there, while the arms appear at Tuṅgnāth, the face at Rudranāth, the navel (or belly) at Madhyamaheśvar and the matted hair at Kalpeśvar. The Pāṇḍava legend is a Garhwali tradition and is not found in the Mahābhārata itself; the shrines are stone temples of the regional Nāgara type whose surviving fabric is generally not securely dated.
limits: The grouping and the bull legend are regional tradition (class 6); they do not date the shrines, which have no securely dated foundation inscriptions.

name: Aṣṭavināyaka (eight Gaṇeśa shrines of Maharashtra)
summary: A pilgrimage circuit of eight Gaṇeśa temples around Pune in Maharashtra — Morgaon, Siddhatek, Pali, Mahad, Theur, Lenyadri, Ozar and Ranjangaon — each holding a self-manifest (svayambhū) image with its own legend.
details: Tradition prescribes a fixed sequence beginning and ending at Morgaon (Mayureśvara), the principal seat of the Gāṇapatya tradition, whose mythology is set out in the Gaṇeśa and Mudgala Purāṇas. The temples in their present form are mostly 17th–18th-century Marāṭhā-period buildings or rebuildings, several of them patronised by the Peśvās and their officials.
limits: The circuit is a devotional grouping whose present form is early modern; the svayambhū images and their legends are temple tradition.

name: Navagraha temples of the Kaveri delta
summary: A set of nine temples near Kumbakonam and Mayiladuthurai in Tamil Nadu, each associated in tradition with one of the nine planetary deities (navagraha); eight are Śiva temples with a graha shrine, and only Sūryanār Kōvil is dedicated to the graha (Sūrya) as principal deity.
details: Members and their grahas: Sūryanār Kōvil (Sūrya), Tiṅkaḷūr (Candra), Vaitīsvaran Kōvil (Aṅgāraka/Mars), Tiruveṇkāṭu (Budha), Āluṅkuṭi (Guru/Bṛhaspati), Kañcaṉūr (Śukra), Tirunaḷḷāṟu (Śani), Tirunāgeśvaram (Rāhu) and Kīḻapperumpaḷḷam (Ketu). Most are Cōḻa-period Śiva temples that also appear among the Tēvāram shrines; the grouping of the nine as a planetary circuit is a later devotional and astrological practice whose origin is not securely dated.
limits: The planetary association is temple tradition; the date at which the nine were grouped as a circuit is not established in the sources consulted.

name: Ahom kingdom
summary: Kingdom of the Brahmaputra valley (Assam) founded by Tai-speaking Ahoms in the 13th century; its later kings, notably Gadādhar Siṃha and Śiva Siṃha, patronised Śaiva and Śākta temples around Guwahati.

name: Māṇikya dynasty of Tripura
summary: Ruling house of the kingdom of Tripura (Twipra) from the 15th century until 1949; Dhanya Māṇikya is credited with founding the Tripura Sundarī temple at Udaipur.

name: Kingdom of Manipur
summary: Meitei kingdom of the Manipur valley; from the 18th century its rulers adopted Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism and built the royal Govindajī temple at Imphal.

dates.label: c. 12th c.–1949 CE (standard chronology; earlier dates are traditional)

name: Utpala dynasty of Kashmir
summary: Kashmiri dynasty founded by Avantivarman (r. c. 855–883), builder of the Avantisvāmin and Avantīśvara temples at Avantipura; its history is told in Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī.

name: Gurjara-Pratīhāra dynasty
summary: North Indian imperial dynasty (c. 8th–11th c.) based at Kanauj, under whose rule many of the early Māru-Gurjara and central Indian Nāgara temples (Osian, Bateshwar) were built.

name: Kacchapaghāta dynasty
summary: Dynasty of the Gwalior region (c. 10th–12th c.); a later inscription at Mitaoli associates the circular Causaṭh Yoginī temple with the Kacchapaghāta king Devapāla.

name: Kalacuris of Tripurī
summary: Dynasty of the upper Narmadā valley (Ḍāhala), with its capital at Tripurī near Jabalpur, c. 7th–13th c.; the Bhedaghat Causaṭh Yoginī temple and the early temples at Amarkantak are attributed to their period.

name: Bundelā kingdom of Orchha
summary: Rajput state of Bundelkhand founded in 1531 with its capital at Orchha; its rulers built the Rām Rājā and Caturbhuj temples.

name: Marāṭhā state (Chhatrapatis and Peśvās)
summary: The Marāṭhā state founded by Śivājī (crowned 1674), later directed by the Peśvās from Pune until 1818; Marāṭhā rulers, ministers and generals rebuilt or endowed many temples across western and northern India.

name: Kingdom of Mysore (Woḍeyar dynasty)
summary: South Indian kingdom ruled by the Woḍeyars (with the interregnum of Haidar ʿAlī and Ṭīpū Sulṭān), patrons of the Cāmuṇḍeśvarī temple on Chamundi Hill.

name: Cāḷukyas of Kalyāṇī (Western Cāḷukyas)
summary: Deccan dynasty (973–1189) whose ornate temples at Lakkundi, Itagi and elsewhere define the “Kalyāṇī Cāḷukya” or later Cāḷukya style.

name: Cāḷukyas of Veṅgī (Eastern Cāḷukyas)
summary: Dynasty of coastal Andhra (c. 624–1070) to whom the Bhīmeśvara temple at Draksharama is attributed.

name: Malla kings of Mallabhūm (Bishnupur)
summary: Bengal dynasty of Mallabhūm whose 17th-century Vaiṣṇava rulers, converts under Śrīnivāsa Ācārya’s influence, built the brick and laterite temples of Bishnupur.

dates.label: c. 16th c.–1806 CE (earlier dates are traditional)

name: Mughal empire
summary: Empire of the Timurid Mughals (1526–1857); under Akbar Hindu nobles such as Mān Siṃh of Amber built major temples (Govindadeva at Vrindavan, 1590), while some later rulers ordered temples demolished.

name: Kachvāhā kingdom of Amber (Jaipur)
summary: Rajput kingdom of Amber, later Jaipur; its rulers served the Mughals and patronised Kṛṣṇa temples in Braj and, from 1714–35, rehoused the Govindadeva image at Jaipur.

dates.label: 16th c.–1949 CE (as a Mughal-allied state; earlier origins traditional)

name: Shah dynasty of Nepal
summary: The Gorkha (Shah) dynasty that unified Nepal from 1768 until the abolition of the monarchy in 2008; patrons of Kathmandu valley shrines such as Manakāmanā and Dakṣiṇkālī.

name: Jaffna kingdom (Āryacakravarti dynasty)
summary: Tamil kingdom of northern Sri Lanka (c. 13th c.–1619) under the Āryacakravartis; tradition and the Yālppāṇa Vaipava Mālai credit it with the first Nallur Kandaswamy temple.

name: Chenla
summary: Khmer polity (6th–8th c.) known from Chinese sources and Sanskrit and Khmer inscriptions; Īśānavarman I’s capital Īśānapura is identified with Sambor Prei Kuk.

name: Pagan kingdom
summary: Burmese kingdom centred on Bagan (c. 849–1297); among its thousands of Buddhist monuments the Nathlaung Kyaung is the one surviving Vaiṣṇava temple.

name: Majapahit
summary: East Javanese kingdom (1293–c. 1527) whose state temple Penataran carries Rāmāyaṇa and Kṛṣṇāyana reliefs.

name: Irukkuvēḷ chiefs of Kodumbalur
summary: Tamil chiefly family of Kodumbalur, allies and feudatories of the early Cōḻas, to whom the Mūvarkōvil temples are attributed by inscription.

name: Śailodbhava dynasty
summary: Dynasty of Koṅgoda in coastal Odisha (c. 6th–8th c.) under whom the earliest surviving Bhubaneswar temples, including Paraśurāmeśvara, were built.

name: Bhauma-Kara dynasty
summary: Dynasty of Odisha (c. 8th–10th c.) with Śākta and Buddhist patronage; the Vaitāl Deul at Bhubaneswar is generally placed in their period.

name: Guhilas of Mewar
summary: Rajput dynasty of Mewar (Guhilas, later Sisodiyās), whose rulers style themselves the dīvān (regent) of Ekaliṅgajī, the tutelary Śiva of the Eklingji temple.

name: Umānanda temple, Guwahati
summary: Śiva temple on Umananda (Peacock) Island in the Brahmaputra at Guwahati, first built in 1694 on the orders of the Ahom king Gadādhar Siṃha; badly damaged in the 1897 Assam earthquake and later rebuilt.
details: The island hill is called Bhasmācala in local tradition, which places here Śiva’s burning of Kāma to ashes (bhasma). Contemporary accounts summarised in the sources state that the brick temple was raised in 1694 by the Barphukan Garhganya Handique at the order of Gadādhar Siṃha (r. 1681–1696). The 1897 earthquake wrecked it; the present building is a later reconstruction by a local merchant, whose interior carries Vaiṣṇava inscriptions.

name: Hayagrīva Mādhava temple, Hajo
summary: Viṣṇu temple on Maṇikūṭa hill at Hajo near Guwahati whose present stone building is attributed to the Koch ruler Raghudeva Nārāyaṇa (late 16th c.); it is also revered by some Buddhists as the place of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
details: The temple stands on a high plinth with a frieze of elephants and wall reliefs of the ten avatāras and episodes from the epics. The image is worshipped as Mādhava with Hayagrīva associations. Bhutanese and Tibetan Buddhist pilgrims have long identified the site with Kuśinagara, a reattribution recorded in later Buddhist pilgrimage literature; Hajo is accordingly a shared Hindu–Buddhist (and, with the nearby Poa Mecca, Muslim) pilgrimage centre.

summary: Ruined complex of stone temples at Baihata Chariali near Guwahati, dated on stylistic grounds to about the 10th–12th centuries, with erotic and divine sculpture associated in local tradition with Kāmadeva.

name: Tripura Sundarī temple, Udaipur (Tripura)
summary: Śākta temple on a tortoise-backed hillock at Udaipur, Tripura, founded according to tradition by Mahārāja Dhanya Māṇikya around 1501; counted among the 51 Śakti pīṭhas as the place where Satī’s right foot fell.
details: The temple is a single-cell building of the Bengali ek-ratna type with a curved roof. The state of Tripura is popularly said to take its name from the goddess. Animal sacrifice, part of the temple’s worship, was halted for some weeks in 2019 by a court order and then resumed. The adjoining Kalyāṇ Sāgar tank keeps tortoises sacred to the shrine.

name: Unakoti rock reliefs
summary: Śaiva rock-cut reliefs and loose images on a forested hill near Kailashahar, Tripura, ascribed on stylistic grounds to the 7th–9th centuries; the central Unakotīśvara Kāla Bhairava head is about 9 m high.
details: The name “one less than a crore” comes from a legend in which Śiva, travelling to Kāśī with 99,99,999 gods, cursed them to stone when they overslept. Besides the colossal Śiva head flanked by female figures (one identified as Durgā on a lion), the site has large Gaṇeśa reliefs. The only inscription, on a caturmukha liṅga, is in Bengali characters of the 11th–12th centuries and names one Śrī Jayadeva, probably a pilgrim. The site is protected by the ASI and was placed on India’s UNESCO Tentative List in 2022.

name: Śrī Govindajī temple, Imphal
summary: Royal Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava temple of Rādhā-Govinda beside the old palace of the Manipur kings at Imphal; first built in 1846, rebuilt after an 1868 earthquake and reconsecrated in 1876, with the images reinstalled in the present temple in 1908.
details: Manipuri tradition holds that King Bhāgyacandra (r. 1763–1798) had the image of Govindajī carved after a vision and consecrated it in 1779 in his palace. Mahārāja Nara Siṃh commissioned a temple on 16 January 1846; it was rebuilt to the same design under Candrakīrti and consecrated on 26 April 1876. After the Anglo-Manipur war of 1891 the images were moved and in 1908 were reconsecrated in the present temple by Mahārāja Churachand Siṃh. The temple is the centre of Manipuri Vaiṣṇava ritual, including the rāsa-līlā dance.

summary: Nāgara Śiva temple at Baijnath in the Kangra valley, built in 1204 CE by two merchants, Ahuka and Manyuka, according to its own inscriptions; Śiva is worshipped as Vaidyanātha, “lord of physicians”.

name: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa temple group, Chamba
summary: Group of stone śikhara temples with wooden canopies in Chamba town, Himachal Pradesh, whose main Viṣṇu temple is attributed to Rājā Sāhila Varman, the 10th-century founder of Chamba; a gilded finial was added in 1678.

A metal Garuḍa stands on the pillar before the main shrine, and Rājā Chatar Siṃh added gold-plated pinnacles in 1678.

name: Masrur rock-cut temples
summary: Monolithic complex of Nāgara temples carved from a sandstone ridge in the Kangra valley in the early 8th century, dedicated chiefly to Śiva with Viṣṇu, Devī and Sūrya imagery; unfinished and earthquake-damaged.

Much sculpture is lost and the complex was left incomplete.

name: Amarnāth cave
summary: Glacial cave at about 3,888 m in the Lidder–Sind watershed of Kashmir where an ice stalagmite is worshipped as a self-formed liṅga of Śiva (Amareśvara); the summer yātrā is one of the largest Himalayan pilgrimages.
details: Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī (12th c.) and the Nīlamata Purāṇa refer to Amareśvara and its pilgrimage. The pilgrimage is administered by a shrine board and opens only in summer.

name: Rani ki Vav (Queen’s Stepwell), Patan
summary: Monumental seven-storey stepwell at Patan, Gujarat, built for the Caulukya queen Udayamatī in the 11th century and conceived as an inverted temple; its walls carry hundreds of sculptures, overwhelmingly Vaiṣṇava, including the avatāras of Viṣṇu. UNESCO World Heritage Site (2014).
details:
Merutuṅga’s Prabandhacintāmaṇi (1304) records that Udayamatī, daughter of Naravarāha Khengāra, built a novel stepwell at Śrīpattana (Patan) surpassing the Sahasraliṅga tank. One account dates its commissioning to 1063 with completion some twenty years later; M. S. Commissariat instead placed it around 1032 by comparison with the Vimala Vasahī at Mount Abu. Silted up by the shifting Sarasvatī, it was cleared in the 1940s and excavated and restored by the ASI between 1981 and 1987.

The sculptural programme turns the descending galleries into a temple to water: Viṣṇu in many forms, the daśāvatāra, Śeṣaśāyī Viṣṇu at the well end, goddesses, apsarās and nāga-kanyās. The site is ASI monument N-GJ-160.

name: Ekaliṅgajī temple, Kailashpuri

name: Śrīnāthjī temple, Nathdwara

details: Puṣṭimārga tradition holds that the image emerged from Govardhana hill — an arm first appearing in 1410/1466 — and was revealed to Vallabhācārya, who instituted its worship. The temple’s seva follows the daily round of the child Kṛṣṇa, and its painted cloth hangings (picchavāī) and Nathdwara painting form a distinct school. In 1802 the image was briefly taken to Udaipur during the Holkar raids.

name: Kṛṣṇa Janmasthān temple complex, Mathurā
summary: Temple complex in Mathurā built from 1953 (completed 1982) on the site revered as Kṛṣṇa’s birthplace, beside the Shahi Idgah mosque raised after Aurangzeb ordered the great Keśavadeva temple destroyed in 1670; the site has a long history of temple building and destruction and is the subject of ongoing litigation.
details:
Excavations have yielded pottery and terracottas from the 6th century BCE, and Vaiṣṇava worship nearby is attested from the early centuries CE. A Sanskrit inscription found on the site records that in VS 1207 (1150) one Jajja, probably a Gāhaḍavāla vassal, built a Viṣṇu temple there. In the early 17th century the Bundelā ruler Bīr Siṃh Deo built a great Keśavadeva temple (described by European travellers), which was demolished on Aurangzeb’s orders in 1670; the Shahi Idgah mosque stands on part of its site.

The present complex — the Keśavadeva temple, the Garbha Gṛha shrine (the “birth-chamber”) and the Bhāgavata Bhavan — was built from 1953 with funds from the Dalmia and Birla families and completed in 1982. Since 2020 suits concerning the mosque and the land have been before the courts; this record does not take a position on them.

name: Śabarimala Dharmaśāstā (Ayyappan) temple
summary: Hill shrine of Ayyappan (Dharmaśāstā) in the Periyar forests of Kerala, reached by pilgrims after a 41-day vow and the climb of the eighteen sacred steps; restored after a fire in 1902 and rebuilt after an arson attack in 1950, it receives millions of pilgrims in the Maṇḍala–Makaravilakku season.
details:
Ayyappan is held to be the son of Śiva and Mohinī (Viṣṇu’s female form); his cult combines forest, warrior and ascetic traits, and pilgrims of all castes and religions take the same vow, addressing each other as “Swami”. The sanctum roof is gold-plated.

The temple’s custom of excluding women aged about 10–50 was struck down by the Supreme Court of India on 28 September 2018 (Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala); review petitions were referred to a larger bench in 2019, and the matter remains contested. Radhika Sekar’s study describes the pilgrimage and cult.

name: Bujang Valley candi (Kedah)
summary: Remains of brick and laterite Hindu and Buddhist shrines (candi) in the Bujang Valley of Kedah, Malaysia, part of a trading complex of the 5th–14th centuries; the reconstructed Candi Bukit Batu Pahat is the best-known Śaiva shrine.

name: Ganga Talao (Grand Bassin), Mauritius
summary: Crater lake in southern Mauritius made a Hindu tīrtha after a priest of Triolet, Jhummun Giri, dreamed in 1887 (or the 1890s) that its waters flowed from the Gaṅgā; Gaṅgā water was poured into it in 1972, it was declared a sacred lake in 1998, and the Mahāśivarātri pilgrimage draws hundreds of thousands.
details: The pilgrimage gave descendants of the half-million indentured labourers brought to Mauritius in the 19th century a way to “bathe in sacred waters once more”. Patrick Eisenlohr’s ethnography describes the Śivarātri pilgrimage as central to Mauritian Hindu identity. Shrines line the shore, and a 33 m statue of Śiva (Maṅgal Mahādev) stands at the entrance (2007, recall).

name: Temple in the Sea (Sewdass Sadhu Shiv Mandir), Trinidad
summary: Small Śiva temple on a causeway in the Gulf of Paria at Waterloo, Trinidad, built single-handedly from 1947 to 1952 by Sewdass Sadhu, an indentured labourer from India, after he was refused land; rebuilt and reopened in 1995 for the 150th anniversary of Indian indentured arrival.
details: Sadhu (b. 1901) first built on estate land, from which he was evicted, and then carried stones and sand by bicycle to extend a platform into the sea. Images of Śiva, Durgā, Gaṇeśa, Hanumān and Kṛṣṇa are installed.

name: Yamunā river
